content: Calcium carbonate is an antacid that has been approved by the FDA for the treatment of heartburn, sour stomach, acid indigestion, and upset stomach associated with these symptoms. Common side effects include constipation, flatulence, and abdominal bloating. For adults, calcium carbonate is used to prevent calcium deficiency. The recommended daily allowance (RDA) for individuals aged 19 to 50 years is 1000 mg of elemental calcium per day, divided into doses of 500 mg or less, with a maximum daily intake of 2500 mg. For men aged 51 to 70 years, the RDA remains 1000 mg per day, with a maximum of 2000 mg. For women in the same age group, the RDA increases to 1200 mg per day, with a maximum of 2000 mg. For individuals over 70 years of age, the RDA is 1200 mg per day, divided into doses of 500 mg or less, with a maximum of 2000 mg daily. Off-label uses of calcium carbonate include the treatment of chemical burns caused by hydrofluoric acid, prevention of bone fractures, management of chronic hypocalcemia, treatment of heartburn, and prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis. In pediatric populations, calcium carbonate is also used to prevent calcium deficiency. The RDA for infants aged 0 to 6 months is 200 mg of elemental calcium per day, with a maximum of 1000 mg daily. For infants aged 6 to 12 months, the RDA is 260 mg per day, with a maximum of 1500 mg. For children aged 1 to 3 years, the RDA is 700 mg per day, with a maximum of 2500 mg. For children aged 4 to 8 years, the RDA is 1000 mg per day, with a maximum of 2500 mg. For children aged 9 to 13 years, the RDA is 1300 mg per day, with a maximum of 3000 mg. For adolescents aged 14 to 18 years, the RDA is also 1300 mg per day, with a maximum of 3000 mg. Calcium carbonate should not be used without consulting a healthcare provider if the patient has kidney stones or is on a calcium-restricted diet. Patients taking prescription medications should consult a doctor or pharmacist before using calcium carbonate, as antacids may interact with certain drugs. The maximum dosage of calcium carbonate should not exceed 10 tablets in 24 hours, and the maximum dosage should not be used for more than two weeks. This product should be kept out of reach of children. Common adverse reactions include gastrointestinal symptoms such as constipation, flatulence, and abdominal bloating. Serious adverse effects may include myocardial infarction, urolithiasis, prostate cancer, and milk-alkali syndrome. There is no specific FDA guidance on the use of calcium carbonate during pregnancy, labor and delivery, nursing, or in pediatric, geriatric, or immunocompromised populations. Similarly, there is no specific guidance on its use in patients with renal or hepatic impairment, or in relation to gender or race. Calcium carbonate is administered orally. There is limited information available regarding its mechanism of action, pharmacodynamics, pharmacokinetics, and nonclinical toxicology. In cases of suspected overdose, the National Poison Help hotline (1-800-222-1222) should be contacted immediately. Calcium carbonate should be stored at a temperature of 20 to 25°C (68 to 77°F). There is no established interaction between calcium carbonate and alcohol, but patients should consult their healthcare provider regarding alcohol use while taking this medication.
